peptide.name: NAD+
peptide.summary: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is an essential coenzyme found in every living cell, required for cellular energy (ATP) production, DNA repair, and as a substrate for sirtuin enzymes involved in aging biology. It is not a peptide (it is a dinucleotide) but is widely marketed alongside peptides as an IV or subcutaneous infusion for energy, cognition, and anti-aging. It is not FDA-approved as a drug for any of these marketed indications; controlled human trial evidence for IV/injectable NAD+ specifically is limited.
peptide.description: NAD+ is composed of two nucleotides joined by a pyrophosphate bond: one bearing adenine, the other bearing nicotinamide. It exists in oxidized (NAD+) and reduced (NADH) forms and cycles between them as a central electron carrier in cellular respiration, making it essential for mitochondrial ATP production. Beyond energy metabolism, NAD+ is a required substrate for sirtuins (NAD-dependent deacetylases implicated in aging and metabolic regulation), PARP enzymes involved in DNA repair, and CD38, which consumes NAD+ and whose activity increases with age -- a proposed mechanism for the age-related decline in tissue NAD+ levels that underlies much of the 'NAD+ boosting' longevity marketing. Unlike its precursors nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which are sold as oral supplements with a larger human trial base, direct IV or subcutaneous NAD+ administration has a much thinner controlled-trial evidence base; most published human data are small, short-term tolerability/pilot studies rather than large randomized efficacy trials for any of the commercially marketed benefits (energy, cognition, hangover recovery, anti-aging).
peptide.mechanism_of_action: Functions as a coenzyme carrying electrons in oxidation-reduction reactions central to mitochondrial ATP synthesis (glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation). Serves as an obligate substrate for sirtuin deacetylases, PARP DNA-repair enzymes, and NAD-glycohydrolases (e.g., CD38), linking cellular NAD+ availability to energy metabolism, genomic stability, and proposed aging pathways.

half_life.note: Exogenous NAD+ has poor cell permeability and is rapidly metabolized; plasma kinetics after IV infusion are not well standardized across the commercial IV-therapy literature.

peptide.evidence_note: NAD+'s role in fundamental cell biology (energy metabolism, DNA repair, sirtuin activity) is well established in basic science. However, evidence specifically supporting IV/injectable NAD+ administration for the marketed consumer benefits (energy, cognitive enhancement, anti-aging, addiction/hangover recovery) is limited to small pilot and tolerability studies rather than large controlled efficacy trials. Do not conflate general NAD+ biology evidence with proof that infusions deliver the marketed effects.
peptide.fda_status_note: Not FDA-approved as a drug for any indication. IV/injectable NAD+ is offered by wellness clinics and IV-therapy providers, typically under general supplement or compounding frameworks rather than as an approved pharmaceutical.
peptide.compounding_note: Often supplied via compounding pharmacies for IV-therapy clinics; regulatory oversight varies. Not FDA-approved as a finished drug product.

benefits.label: Cellular energy metabolism (established basic biology)
benefits.detail: Central, well-established role as an electron carrier in mitochondrial ATP production.

benefits.label: DNA repair / sirtuin substrate (established basic biology)
benefits.detail: Required substrate for PARP DNA-repair enzymes and sirtuin deacetylases implicated in aging and metabolic regulation.

benefits.label: Subjective energy / cognition (marketed, thin clinical evidence)
benefits.detail: Small pilot/tolerability studies of IV NAD+ report some metabolic changes (e.g., HDL-C, ALP) over short follow-up, but data are preliminary and exploratory outcomes were variable; not established efficacy for marketed cognitive/energy claims.

risks.label: Infusion discomfort
risks.detail: IV NAD+ infusions are commonly reported to cause tightness in the chest, cramping, or flushing, especially with rapid infusion rates.

risks.label: Limited controlled human efficacy data
risks.detail: Marketed benefits substantially outrun the available randomized controlled trial evidence for injectable/IV administration specifically.

risks.label: Variable clinic/compounding quality
risks.detail: IV-therapy providers vary in sourcing, sterility practices, and dosing consistency.

side_effects.label: Flushing / chest tightness with rapid infusion

contraindications.label: Pregnancy and lactation
contraindications.detail: Insufficient data on IV/injectable administration; avoid.

reconstitution.note: Typically supplied as a solution for IV infusion or subcutaneous injection by a clinic, rather than as a lyophilized powder for self-reconstitution. Infusion rate (not just total dose) affects tolerability.

lyophilized.stability: NAD+ solutions are light- and temperature-sensitive; degrade over time.

peptide.disclaimer: For research and educational purposes only. This is not medical advice. NAD+ is not a peptide and is not FDA-approved as a drug for any marketed indication. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using IV or injectable NAD+.

dose_ranges.context: IV/subcutaneous NAD+ therapy (clinic-reported ranges) — NOT independently validated for marketed claims
dose_ranges.frequency: weekly to several times per week (clinic-dependent)
dose_ranges.note: Wide range reported across IV-therapy providers; total dose and infusion rate both affect tolerability. No standardized, trial-validated dosing exists for any of the marketed consumer benefits.

protocols.name: IV infusion (clinic-reported pattern)
protocols.description: IV-therapy clinics commonly administer NAD+ as a slow infusion over 1-4+ hours, sometimes starting with lower doses/slower rates to assess tolerability before increasing. Summarized only to document the reported pattern, not as guidance.

dosing.frequency: weekly to several times per week (clinic-dependent)

protocols.cycling_notes: No validated cycling protocol exists; typically ongoing per clinic recommendation.
protocols.disclaimer: Informational summary of clinic-reported practice. Not medical advice or a dosing recommendation.
